first_remarks.remarks_to_the_author:
This paper contains important information for related researchers as it presents a method to maximize energy storage efficiency using defect control and crystal orientation techniques in NBT-SBT materials. This paper can be published after revision, but corrections/explanations are required for the following matters:

1. The sentence "This disparity can be attributed to the lower electrostriction coefficient Q33 of ABO3 perovskite crystals in the <111> direction compared to other directions" on line 252 requires appropriate references and a more detailed explanation. Samples textured in the <111> direction have a smaller polarization value than other samples but have a higher energy storage capacity because they have strong dielectric breakdown strength and can withstand a high electric field. Therefore, in this paper, it is considered very important to analyze why samples aligned in the <111> direction have high dielectric breakdown strength. The authors need to provide a more detailed analysis and explanation on this part. They claim that, in general, the electric strain coefficient (Q33) in the <111> direction in the perovskite structure is smaller than in other directions. However, in the perovskite structure, the electric strain coefficient along the direction may vary depending on the crystal structure (rhombohedral, orthorhombic, tetragonal, etc.). Therefore, a more detailed explanation is needed regarding the crystal structure and direction-dependent electrical strain characteristics of the BNT-BST material synthesized in this study. Additionally, another reason why the dielectric breakdown strength of the perovskite structure varies depending on the crystal direction may be the difference in atomic density and interatomic bonding force depending on the crystal direction. The authors need to provide a more logical explanation as to why the <111> oriented samples have higher dielectric strength than randomly oriented samples or ceramic samples with crystals oriented in the <001> direction. One of the important technologies in future ceramic processing is crystal orientation technology. Changes in dielectric breakdown characteristics and the electrical properties of ceramics oriented in various crystal directions are crucial information in the ceramic device industry. Therefore, a more detailed and logical explanation is needed.
2. In Figure 5(e), it was calculated that the sample in the <111> direction had a higher Wrec value than the sample in the <001> direction under the same electric field conditions. However, in the P-E loop in Figure 5(a), the polarization value of the sample in the <111> direction is smaller than the polarization value of the sample in the <001> direction. How can a sample in the <111> direction have a higher Wrec value than a sample in the <001> direction under the same electric field?
3. Since NBT is a single phase, it would be better to express it as Na1/2Bi1/2TiO3 rather than Na0.5Bi0.5TiO3.
4. Since the MLCC samples also have the composition of 0.65NBT-0.35SBT doped with Mn, it would be appropriate to express '0.65NBT-0.35SBT matrix' in line 247 of the text as '0.5 mol% Mn-doped 0.65NBT-0.35SBT matrix'.
5. The authors represented the recoverable energy storage density as follows:
6. W\_rec=∫\_(P\_r)^(P\_max) EdP

This is an incorrect mathematical formula for Wrec. Although the positive integral of an electric field with respect to polarization from remnant polarization (Pr) to saturated polarization (Pmax) seems to be identical to the negative integral of an electric field with respect to polarization from Pmax to Pr mathematically, the positive integral cannot be equal to the negative integral due to the hysteretic characteristic of ferroelectrics/piezoelectrics in reality. As the authors probably know, the upward path in a hysteresis loop from Pr to Pmax is never identical to the downward path from Pmax to Pr. Hence, Wrec should be represented as shown in [Ceram. Inter. 47 (2021) 23488; Adv. Funct. Mater 29 (2019) 1807321]: W\_rec=-∫\_(P\_max)^(P\_r) EdP

6. When synthesizing from <111>-BaTiO3 templates to <111>-SrTiO3 templates using the topochemical reaction method, Ba compound residues will remain. Also, when synthesizing from Bi4Ti3O12 templates to <001>-SrTiO3 templates, Bi compound residues will remain. How did the author remove these residual compounds?
7. Sometimes, the characteristics of the final synthesized material may vary depending on the difference in starting materials. Therefore, it is necessary to provide the manufacturer and model name of the starting materials for synthesizing Mn-doped NBT-SBT ceramic and <001>- and <111>-SrTiO3 template particles.
The manuscript is well written and has scientific interest. It may be accepted in its present form.

Manuscript Title: Enhanced energy storage density and efficiency in NBT-based MLCCs via a cooperative optimization of polarization and grain alignment

Authours: Yang Li, Ningbo Fan, Jie Wu, Bin Xu, Xuexin Li, Xuechen Liu, Yizhou Xiao, Dingwei Hou, Xinya Feng, Jinjing Zhang, Shujun Zhang, Jinglei Li & Fei Li

Authours have prepared (1-x)(0.65Na0.5Bi0.5TiO3-0.35Sr0.7Bi0.2TiO3)-xMnO2 (x = 0, 0.5 mol%, 1 mol%, and 1.5 mol%) using solid-state reaction method. Four ceramics samples were characterised by XPS, EPR, P-E loop, dielectric measurements as a function frequency and temperature, XRD patterns as a function of temperature, Rietveld refinements for RT-XRD data and Raman spectra. Based on the increase in polarisation maximum, decrease in remnant polarisation and decrease in hysteresis loss, x=0.5 mol% MnO2 substituted sample was selected to further optimisation of the energy storage density. For this, non-textured, <001>-textured and <111>- textured MLCC capacitors with 5 effective layers were prepared through tedious preparation process and analyzed by XRD pattern, SEM micrographs, elemental mapping, EBSD, P-E loop, S-E loop, breakdown strength and discharge-time curves. Wrec, �, Eb and Wdis were calculated. Further, temperature dependent (-100 to 200oC) unipolar P-E loop and fatigue performance up to 10^6 cycles were also measured.

The main results of the manuscript are that 5 wt% SrTiO3 flakes added <111>-textured MLCC capacitors exhibit η, Eb and Wdis respectively 95%, 850 kV/cm and 15.7 J/cm3(Figure 5(i)) and the main finding is that increasing the breakdown strength (Eb) through texturing plays a major role to improve the energy storage density rather than increase of Pmax. For achieving ultrahigh energy storage density and efficiency, the manuscript may be considered with a mandatory major revision.

- (1) DFPT calculation was carried out to obtain changes in the polarisation due to Mn-substitution. A 2x2x2 supercell with 40 atoms and 8 Formula units were taken for the calculation. The calculation was done for the composition Na0.5Bi0.5Ti0.875Mn0.125O3. However, from the experiments, the best results were obtained for 0.995(0.65Na0.5Bi0.5TiO3-0.35Sr0.7Bi0.2TiO3)-0.005MnO2 composition. Experimental composition and computational composition are in no way close to each another. Sr was not included for the calculation. Authours should have taken Na0.32Bi0.38Sr0.24Ti0.995Mn0.005O3 as the composition for computation. Four Bi, two Na and two Sr should have taken for each unit cell. Further, 6x6x6 supercell, one Ti may be replaced by Mn. This could be a close composition for the calculation to match the experimental composition and to explain the experimental observation. Enthalpy of formation for Mn2+, Mn3+, Mn4+, Ti3+ and Ti4+ should be comparable and this data was not given in the manuscript to ascertain that on Mn2+ substitution, system is a minimum energy configuration. Mn2+ substitution improves the polarisation is not universal result that can be applied for all perovskite systems. Therefore, computational results and experimental results may not be connected for discussion, even if the authors' write 'as an example' (page 6, line 106). Therefore, computational results and the relevant discussion should be completely removed from the manuscript and accordingly whole of the manuscript may be revised.
- (2) Was there a Mn peak in XPS? Please include it in the manuscript (or) supplementary.
- (3) Large number of pores is seen in the SEM cross-section micrograph in both textured samples. Why pores are formed at large numbers in textured sample compared to non-textured sample? How to study the impact of pores on the energy storage density?

The paper of Yang Li et al. " Enhanced energy storage density and efficiency in NBT-based MLCCs via a cooperative optimization of polarization and grain alignment" presents a synergistic optimization strategy that combine polarization and grain alignment engineering. As per my observation, the manuscript over all is well written and the experimental results are well analyzed. However, the manuscript needs a revision to address several points list below before I could recommend it for publication. The comments are listed below:

Comment 1: Born effective charge of Mn2+ (2.66 e) is smallest among the Ti3+, Ti4+, Mn4+, Mn3+ and the binding energy is maximum. Then, Why Mn2+ causes such a significant increase in off-centering displacements compared to Mn4+ and Mn3+?

Comment 2: How were the different valence states of Mn (Mn4+, Mn3+, and Mn2+) confirmed experimentally under hightemperature sintering conditions?

Comment 3: It is noted that Mn doping at 0.5 mol% results in the highest Ti4+ content, with subsequent doping levels gradually reducing Ti4+ but still maintaining levels higher than the undoped sample.

Comment 4: In EPR, authors claim 0.5 mol% Mn doped component shows only one type of signal, corresponding to Mn2+ and 1 mol% Mn exhibits both Mn2+ and Mn4+ signals. It is difficult to distinguish the between the EPR of 0.5% and 1.0% spectrum. How were Mn2+ and 4+ valence states identified in the 1 mol% Mn doped? Could the authors elaborate on the characteristics of this signal and why it is specific to Mn2+ in 0.5 mol%?

Comment 5: How does the presence of a secondary phase and changes in grain orientation specifically affect the hysteresis and energy storage performance of Mn-doped 0.65NBT-0.35SBT?

Comment 6: In figure 3d, with the % of Mn doping the dielectric constant increases. What is the reason for this enhancement of dielectric constant?

Comment 7: The Temperature dependent dielectric curve shows broadness and frequency dependent behaviour which is the characteristics of relaxor ferroelectric. The author could calculate the diffusivity parameter to estimate the relaxor nature and relate with the polarization behaviour of samples.

Comment 8: What is the reason for synthesizing flaky Ba6Ti17O40 precursor to acquire the <111>-oriented SrTiO3 flake microcrystalline template?

Comment 9: Describe the relationship between the structural variation of <100> and <111> and the difference in polarization values between them.

Comment 10: Perhaps the authors could have also cite other relevant articles, such as EPR and magnetization studies of the manganites (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmmm.2020.167450), https://doi.org/10.1088/2053-1591/2/9/096301, and https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4804940,

DOI 10.1088/1361-6463/aa7fa7, https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4862169 etc.

unsorted.remarks_to_the_author: The authors have provided thorough and meaningful responses to the reviewers' comments and have revised the manuscript accordingly. Therefore, the paper is deemed suitable for publication.

The main point raised in the review report was that "Why DFPT calculation was not carried out on a composition close to that of experimental composition?". Authours have pointed out that the DFPT calculation was carried out on Na1/2Bi1/2TiO3 as it is major component (65%) and also due to the computational challenge involved in terms of reasonably large super cell to match the experimental composition. Further, the computational result is that Mn2+ substitution improves the polarisation. This result was compared only qualitatively to the selected experimental composition. Authours reply may be considered positively.

Authors have addressed the comments in details. It can be accepted.

## Reviewer #1:

This paper contains important information for related researchers as it presents a method to maximize energy storage efficiency using defect control and crystal orientation techniques in NBT-SBT materials. This paper can be published after revision, but corrections/explanations are required for the following matters:

1. The sentence 'This disparity can be attributed to the lower electrostriction coefficient Q 33 of ABO3 perovskite crystals in the <111> direction compared to other directions' on line 252 requires appropriate references and a more detailed explanation. Samples textured in the <111> direction have a smaller polarization value than other samples but have a higher energy storage capacity  because  they  have  strong  dielectric  breakdown  strength  and  can  withstand  a  high electric field. Therefore, in this paper, it is considered very important to analyze why samples aligned in the <111> direction have high dielectric breakdown strength. The authors need to provide a more detailed analysis and explanation on this part. They claim that, in general, the electric strain coefficient ( Q 33) in the <111> direction in the perovskite structure is smaller than in other directions. However, in the perovskite structure, the electric strain coefficient along the direction may vary depending on the crystal structure (rhombohedral, orthorhombic, tetragonal, etc.).  Therefore,  a  more  detailed  explanation  is  needed  regarding  the  crystal  structure  and direction-dependent electrical strain characteristics of the BNT-BST material synthesized in this

study. Additionally,  another reason  why the dielectric  breakdown strength of the perovskite structure varies depending on the crystal direction may be the difference in atomic density and interatomic bonding force depending on the crystal direction. The authors need to provide a more logical explanation as to why the <111> oriented samples have higher dielectric strength than  randomly  oriented  samples  or  ceramic  samples  with  crystals  oriented  in  the  <001> direction. One of the important technologies in future ceramic processing is crystal orientation technology.  Changes  in  dielectric  breakdown  characteristics  and  the  electrical  properties  of ceramics oriented in various crystal directions are crucial information in the ceramic device industry. Therefore, a more detailed and logical explanation is needed.

## Author's response:

Thank  you  very  much  for  your  comment.  Electrostriction  is  present  in  all  crystal symmetries  because  it  is  a  fourth  rank  polar  tensor.  Electrostriction  is  a  measure  of  the polarization induced by ions shifting away from their natural equilibrium positions, giving rise to variations in the lattice parameters. A typical potential of an ion-pair is shown in Figure R1, where the energy required to compress the ion-pair is higher than the energy required to extend the ion pair [ N. W. Ashcroft and N. D. Mermin, Solid State Physics (Brooks Cole, Philadelphia, 1976); C. Kittel, Introduction to Solid State Physics, 8th ed. (Wiley, New York, 2004)]. Based on the potential characteristics, the relative displacement between positive and negative ions is prone to occur via extension of the lattice instead of compression.

[Figure redacted]

Figure R1. Schematic figure of the pair potential in ionic crystal, where represents the equilibrium distance between positive and negative ions. [Applied Physics Reviews 1, 011103 (2014)]

Figure R2 shows the variation in the oxygen octahedral structure as polarization appeared

along  different  crystallographic  directions.  When  a  B-site  cation  moves  along  the  [001] direction, an oxygen anion O1 will be 'pushed' upward to release the energy that originated from compressing the distance of B-O1, as shown in Figure R2(b). Consequently, the lattice parameter along the [001] direction is elongated by d. The strain along the [001] direction can be expressed as d/a .

[Figure redacted]

Figure R2. The deformation of oxygen-octahedral structure with different polarization directions. (a) Zero polarization; (b) polarization along [001] direction; (c) polarization along [110] direction; (d) polarization along  [111]  direction.  The  red  arrows  for  oxygen  ions  indicate  that  the  oxygen  ions  move  along  the polarization direction. The purple arrows for oxygen ions indicate that oxygen ions move along the direction perpendicular to the polarization direction. [Applied Physics Reviews 1, 011103 (2014)]

Figure R2(c) shows the scenario where a B-site cation moves along the [110] direction. In this case, the oxygen O3 and O4 anions will move along the [110] or [11 \_ 0]/[1 \_ 10] directions to release the B-O3 and B-O4 pair potential because the direction of B-O bond (<100>) is not parallel to the [110] direction. It should be noted that the electrostrictive coefficient Q 33 along the [110] direction is reduced by the motion of the O3/O4 ions along the [11 \_ 0]/[1 \_ 10] directions, because the [11 \_ 0]/[1 \_ 10] directions are perpendicular to the [110] direction.

Analogous to the [110] direction, a similar scenario occurs for the [111] direction, as shown in Figure R2(d). As a B-site cation moves along the [111] direction, the oxygen ions can move along the directions perpendicular to [111] direction to release the B-O pair potential, which

mitigates  the Q 33  along  the  [111]  direction.  The  difference  between  the  [111]  and  [110] directions is that in the former, the oxygen ions are easier to move along the perpendicular direction to release the compression energy. This is because the angle between the [111] and BO chain directions  is  54°,  which  is  larger  than  the  angle  between  the  [110]  and  B-O  bond directions (45°). Based on this approach, electrostrictive anisotropy of perovskite crystals has been explained qualitatively, which is related to the oxygen octahedral structure. The maximum electrostrictive coefficient Q 33 is along the <001> direction because the B-O chains align along the <111> direction. The minimum Q 33 is along the <111> direction because the B-O chains have a larger angle with the <111> direction.

From a mechanical perspective, the strains and elastic energies induced by applied electric fields  heavily  impact  the  electromechanical  breakdown  strength  of  dielectric  ceramics. Perovskite ceramics are considered brittle solids and thus easily generate microcracks under tensile strains, which may greatly increase the breakdown probability of dielectric ceramics. A high level of tensile strain is expected to induce severe microcracks inside the dielectrics, and is thought to be one of the main reasons that the breakdown strength of perovskite ceramics has reached a plateau over the years. Thus, reducing the field-induced strains is highly desired for further  enhancing  the  energy  density  of  perovskite  materials.  In  perovskite  ceramics,  the maximum Q 33 is along the <001> direction, and the minimum Q 33 is along the <111> direction. <111>-oriented  ceramics  have  smaller  tensile  strain  and  can  withstand  higher  breakdown electric fields than nontextured ceramics and <001>-oriented ceramics.

We apologize for not providing a detailed explanation regarding the content related to Q 33 earlier.  Now,  we  have  added  relevant  statements  and  explanations  in  the  manuscript,  and provided relevant references as evidence support. The following content has been added to the manuscript:

The variations in the octahedral oxygen structure within perovskite materials as a function of  polarization  along  different  crystallographic  directions  are  shown  in  Fig.  S11  of  the Supplementary Information . When Ti 4+ ions at the B site move along the [001] direction, the oxygen ion O1 is  'pushed'  upwards, releasing  energy  due  to  the  compression  of  the Ti-O1 distance. Consequently, the lattice parameter along the [001] direction is extended by a distance d . The strain along the [001] direction is expressed as d/a . When Ti 4+ ions move along the [111]

direction, the oxygen ions can move in a direction perpendicular to the [111] direction, releasing the Ti-O pairs potential and thereby reducing Q 33 along the [111] direction. Compared to the [001] direction, it is easier for oxygen ions to move perpendicularly along the [111] direction to release compressive energy. Thus, the maximum Q 33 is observed along the <001> direction, while the minimum Q 33 is along the <111> direction.

2. In Figure 5(e), it was calculated that the sample in the <111> direction had a higher W rec value than the sample in the <001> direction under the same electric field conditions. However, in the P -E loop in Figure 5(a), the polarization value of the sample in the <111> direction is smaller than the polarization value of the sample in the <001> direction. How can a sample in the <111> direction have a higher W rec value than a sample in the <001> direction under the same electric field?

## Author's response:

Thank you very much for your comment. The reason why <111>-oriented samples have higher W rec compared to <001>-oriented samples under the same electric field is that <111>oriented samples exhibit saturation polarization delay.

The value of W rec is influenced not only by P max, but also by P r, hysteresis, and the degree of delay in saturation polarization (i.e., the time required to reach saturation). Although the polarization value of the sample along the <111>-orientation is a bit smaller than that along the <001>-orientation under the same electric field, the P -E loops shown in Figure 5(a) reveal that the saturation polarization in <111>-oriented samples is delayed compared to <001>-oriented samples. The prepared samples exhibit a mixture of rhombohedral and tetragonal phases, with the  rhombohedral  phase  as  the  primary  crystalline  phase.  Under  an  applied  electric  field, <001>-oriented  rhombohedral  ceramics  exhibit  a  '4R'  engineered  domain  configuration, where the polarization reversal process involves 71° and 109° polarization rotations. In contrast, <111>-oriented  rhombohedral  ceramics  display  a  single-domain  structure,  with  an  ideal polarization reversal involving a 180° rotation. Therefore, compared to <001>-oriented samples, <111>-oriented  samples  are  more  challenging  to  polarize,  resulting  in  a  delayed  saturation polarization. As  a  result,  compared  to  <001>-oriented  samples,  the  <111>-oriented  samples exhibit a greater area under the hysteresis loop, i.e., a higher W rec, for the same electric field

## strength.

Based on the above discussion, we have added the following discussion to the analysis section of Figure 5 in the manuscript:

Although the polarization of the <001>-textured samples is slightly higher than that of the <111>-textured samples under the same electric field, the <111>-textured samples exhibit a higher W rec. This is attributed to the delayed saturation polarization of the hysteresis loops in the  <111>-textured  samples.  Under  an  applied  electric  field,  <001>-oriented  rhombohedral ceramics  exhibit  a  '4R'  engineered  domain  configuration,  where  the  polarization  reversal process involves 71° and 109° polarization rotations. In contrast, <111>-oriented rhombohedral ceramics display a single-domain structure, with an ideal polarization reversal involving a 180° rotation. Therefore, compared to <100>-oriented samples, <111>-oriented samples are more challenging to polarize, resulting in a delayed saturation polarization.

Thank you very much for your comment. We have modified the chemical formula of single-phase NBT from Na0.5Bi0.5TiO3 to Na1/2Bi1/2TiO3 according to your suggestion.

6. When  synthesizing  from  <111>-BaTiO3  templates  to  <111>-SrTiO3  templates  using  the topochemical reaction method, Ba compound residues will remain. Also, when synthesizing from Bi4Ti3O12 templates to <001>-SrTiO3 templates, Bi compound residues will remain. How did the author remove these residual compounds?

## Author's response:

Thank you very much for your comment. The residual Ba compounds and Bi compounds were effectively removed through repeated ultrasonic cleaning in deionized water and pure nitric acid, respectively.

When synthesizing <111>-SrTiO3 templates from <111>-BaTiO3 templates, Ba is present as  BaCl2.  Because  BaCl2  is  highly  soluble  in  water,  it  can  be  effectively  removed  through repeated ultrasonic cleaning with hot deionized water, resulting in pure <111>-SrTiO3 templates. In contrast, when synthesizing <001>-SrTiO3 templates from Bi4Ti3O12 templates, Bi is present as BiCl3. Since BiCl3 is soluble in nitric acid, the product must first be cleaned with pure nitric acid to remove BiCl3. After this, the product should be further cleaned with hot deionized water to ensure complete removal of any remaining contaminants and to obtain pure <001>-SrTiO3 templates.

We apologize for the oversight in the initial experimental section. This detailed procedure has now been added to the 'Methods' section of the manuscript.

7. Sometimes, the characteristics of the final synthesized material may vary depending on the difference in starting materials. Therefore, it is necessary to provide the manufacturer and model name of the starting materials for synthesizing Mn-doped NBT-SBT ceramic and <001>- and <111>-SrTiO3 template particles.

## Author's response:

Thank you very much for your comment. We have added the manufacturer and model name of the starting materials for synthesizing Mn doped NBT-SBT ceramic and<001>- and <111>- SrTiO3 template particles in the 'Methods' of the manuscript.

## Author's response:

Thank you very much for your comment. The SEM cross-sections of textured samples reveal numerous pores due to two primary reasons: first, during the growth process, the grains in  textured  samples  grow  abnormally  along  specific  crystallographic  directions,  which  may result in difficulties to completely fill the pores among grains; second, the grains in textured samples  exhibit  specific  shapes  (as  illustrated  in  Figure  4f  of  the  Manuscript),  leading  to indentations on the fractured surfaces after processing, thereby giving the appearance of pores.

When we try to control crystal orientation in textured ceramics, it is often necessary to sacrifice a certain degree of density, resulting in the presence of pores. In fact, samples with higher density often have higher breakdown electric fields. In order to minimize the influence of pores on the breakdown electric field, we further calcined the sintered textured MLCC in a

mixed atmosphere of argon and oxygen at 1000 °C in a hot isostatic pressing furnace for several hours. The following are the cross-sectional SEM images (Figure R4) of the sintered textured samples before and after heat treatment. Before heat treatment, there were more pores with larger pore sizes, but after heat treatment, the number of pores decreased and the pore size significantly decreased. Therefore, the adverse effect of porosity on energy storage density in textured ceramics can be reduced through heat treatment methods such as hot isostatic pressing and  sintering.  We  have  added  the  SEM  images  of  the  cross-section  of  the  <001>-textured samples before and after heat treatment in a mixed atmosphere to Figure S14 in Supplementary Information for readers to observe the effect of heat treatment more intuitively.

Thank you very much for your comment. The reason why Mn 2+ significantly increases offcentering displacements compared to Mn 4+ and Mn 3+ is that Mn 2+ has the largest ionic radius.

The displacements of the A-site ions, i.e., Na and Bi, are believed to be closely related to ionic radii of the dopants. For instance, the ionic radius of Ti 4+ , Mn 4+ , Mn 3+ , and Mn 2+ is 0.745, 0.670,  0.720,  and  0.970  Å,  respectively.  The  corresponding  tolerance  factors  (defined  as t = r A+ r O √ 2 ( r B+ r O ) ) are shown in Figure R5(a), which exhibit an arc shape with the lowest value given by the Mn 2+ case ( t = 0.770) due to its largest size. As depicted in Figure R5(b) and (c), the average displacements of Na and Bi are inversely related to the variation of the tolerance factor.

Qualitatively similar behaviors are also found in the average displacements of Ti, Mn, and O ions, i.e., a decrease followed by an increase by changing the B-site ion from Ti 4+ to Mn 4+ , Mn 3+ , and Mn 2+ , with the largest value also being from Mn 2+ . Such similarity can be ascribed to interactions between the displacements of the A-site and the displacements of the B-site or O-site atoms. However, the shape of the curve is slightly different from that of the tolerance factor,  e.g.,  with  a  minimum  at  Mn 3+ instead  of  Mn 4+ .  This  subtlety  may  be  related  to  the different  covalency  of  the  chemical  bonds  between  Mn  and  O.  Note  that  octahedrally

coordinated Mn 3+ can have Jahn-Teller distortion (absent in Mn 4+ and Mn 2+ cases), but this Jahn-Teller effect is expected to the weak.

Comment 5: How does the presence of the secondary phase and changes in grain orientation specifically  affect  the  hysteresis  and  energy  storage  performance  of  Mn-doped  0.65NBT0.35SBT?

## Author's response:

Thank you very much for your comment. The presence of the second phase increases the P r, thereby enhancing the hysteresis of the P -E loops, which leads to a simultaneous decrease in W rec and  . Samples with different grain orientations exhibit slight variations in P max under the  same  electric  field,  while  the P r  remains  nearly  unchanged.  Due  to  the  minimal electrostriction  coefficient Q 33  along  the  <111>  direction,  <111>-oriented  samples  can withstand higher breakdown fields, resulting in higher W rec .

The impact of the secondary phase: The current density-electric field curve presented in Supplementary Information Figure S4 demonstrates that excessive Mn doping in NBT-SBTbased ceramics, i.e. doping with 1.5 mol% Mn, leads to a significant broadening of current density peaks due to the formation of a secondary phase, resulting in a pronounced alteration in ferroelectric behavior. Reflected in the hysteresis loop is an increase in hysteresis, with P r suddenly increasing from ~1.6 μC·cm -2 to  5.9 μC·cm -2 ,  resulting in a significant increase in hysteresis loss. An increase in the hysteresis of the hysteresis loop signifies a rise in energy loss, which  adversely  affects  the  attainment  of  high  energy  storage  density  and  efficiency.  We hypothesize that the marked increase in hysteresis may be attributed to interface effects between the secondary phase and the ceramic matrix. As depicted in Figure S7, the secondary phase is primarily  compressed  between  the  ceramic  matrix  grains,  and  the  interfaces  between  the secondary phase and the matrix ceramics might introduce additional polarization effects  or impede  charge  movement,  thereby  enlarging  the  hysteresis  region  of  the  hysteresis  loop. Furthermore, it is acknowledged that the secondary phase could also influence the electrical conductivity. Variations  in  conductivity  can  affect  the  polarization  behavior  of  the  ceramic materials under an electric field, thus altering the hysteresis characteristics of the hysteresis loop. Whether the increased hysteresis is due to interface effects or changes in conductivity necessitates more detailed and comprehensive characterization and analysis, which is not the focus of our current work.

Based on the above analysis, the impact of the second phase on ferroelectric properties has been added to the analysis of Figure 3 in the revised manuscript, as follows:

Upon reaching a doping level of 1.5%, the hysteresis becomes larger, and the P r suddenly increases from ~1.6 μC·cm -2 to 5.9 μC·cm -2 . The current density-electric field curve presented in Suppunderlementary Information Fig. S4 demonstrates that excessive Mn doping in NBTSBT-based  ceramics  leads  to  a  significant  broadening  of  current  density  peaks  due  to  the formation of a secondary phase, resulting in a pronounced alteration in ferroelectric behavior, that is, the hysteresis loss significantly increases.

The impact of the grain orientation: As illustrated in Figure 5a, there is no significant difference in the hysteresis of the hysteresis loops among samples with the same composition but different grain orientations. Variations in grain orientation only affect the P max, with higher P max being favorable for achieving higher energy storage density. However, the enhancement of energy storage density is also influenced by the breakdown electric field; a higher breakdown electric field correlates with increased energy storage density. Electrostriction is a crucial factor determining  the  sample's  ability  to  withstand  the  breakdown  electric  field.  Samples  with different grain orientations exhibit varying electrostriction coefficient Q 33, with the Q 33 being largest in the <001> direction and smallest in the <111> direction. This implies that samples oriented in the <111> direction can endure higher breakdown electric fields. Although the P max in the <111> direction is somewhat reduced, this shortfall is mitigated under high electric fields, resulting in a higher polarization value and, consequently, greater energy storage density for the <111>-oriented ceramics.

The analysis of Figure 5 in the revised manuscript has also been updated to include the influence of grain orientation on ferroelectric properties and energy storage performance, as follows:

Under 500 kV·cm -1 , the strain is notably high for <001>-textured MLCCs, reaching 0.79%, followed by nontextured MLCCs at 0.60%, and the lowest for <111>-textured MLCCs, at only 0.38%. This disparity can be attributed to the lower electrostriction coefficient ( Q 33) of ABO3 perovskite crystals in the <111> direction compared to other directions.

<111>-textured samples achieve the highest W rec, benefiting from both enhanced E B due to reduced tensile strain and a significant increase in P max induced by a high electric field.

The dielectric constant serves as a physical parameter to assess the degree of polarization in a dielectric  material. A  higher  degree  of  polarization  in  the  material  corresponds  to  a  higher dielectric constant. Substituting Mn 2+ at the B-site increases the off-centering displacements of all ions, leading to greater electric displacement (polarization response) under an electric field and thereby enhancing the polarization of the material. Consequently, the components doped with 0.5 mol% and 1 mol% Mn exhibit a larger dielectric constant.

In addition, the significant increase in dielectric constant near T 2 temperature of the 1.5 mol% Mn doped component is attributed to the excess Mn causing abnormalities in the crystal structure, including the generation of secondary phases.

Comment 8: What is the reason for synthesizing flaky Ba6Ti17O40 precursor to acquire the <111>-oriented SrTiO3 flake microcrystalline template?

Author's response:

Thank you very much for your comment. The reason for synthesizing flaky Ba6Ti17O40 precursor is that the metastable Ba6Ti17O40 with monoclinic structure can spontaneously grow in 2D morphology in a molten salt environment. This precursor can then be used to synthesize <111>-oriented BaTiO3 flake template through a reasonable topological microcrystal conversion  method.  Subsequently,  the  <111>-oriented  SrTiO3  template  can  be  obtained  by substituting Ba 2+ with Sr 2+ based on the <111>-oriented BaTiO3 template.

## Author's response:

Thank you very much for your comment. The phase structures of the <100>-oriented and <111>-oriented samples are identical, both featuring a minor presence of the tetragonal phase but  predominantly  composed  of  the  rhombohedral  phase.  However,  in  the  <100>-oriented samples, the grains are aligned along the <100> direction, while in the <111>-oriented samples, the grains are aligned along the <111> direction.

The  influence  of  different  crystal  orientations  on  polarization  is  discussed  using  the rhombohedral  perovskite  crystal  structure  as  an  example.  As  shown  in  Figure  R8,  the polarization direction of the rhombohedral phase is <111>, with eight polarization vectors along the body diagonal: P 1 [11 \_ 1 \_ ], P 2 [1 \_ 1 \_ 1 \_ ], P 3 [1 \_ 11 \_ ], P 4 [111 \_ ], P 1′ [11 \_ 1], P 2′ [1 \_ 1 \_ 1], P 3′ [1 \_ 11] and P 4′ [111]. Taking the (110) plane as an example, when no electric field is applied, the polarization vectors on this plane are P 2 [1 \_ 1 \_ 1 \_ ], P 2′ [1 \_ 1 \_ 1], P 4 [111 \_ ] and P 4′ [111]. Under an applied electric field, <100>-oriented rhombohedral ceramics exhibit a '4R' engineered domain configuration,

where the polarization reversal process involves 71° and 109° polarization rotations. In contrast, <111>-oriented  rhombohedral  ceramics  display  a  single-domain  structure,  with  an  ideal polarization reversal involving a 180° rotation. Therefore, compared to <100>-oriented samples, <111>-oriented  samples  are  more  challenging  to  polarize,  resulting  in  a  delayed  saturation polarization.
